source_span: 5Y auction finished the day with a 3.20bp tail with disappointing end user demand; (iv) 10Y and 5Y yield broke the technical level of 5%.
source_chain: Primary chain (DB Reid, 17530): a 5-year-high composite PMI beat (58.4 vs 55.3) plus an oil rebound signal resilient growth and persistent cost pressure, therefore markets reprice Fed hike odds sharply higher (Oct 53%->71%, year-end 37bps), therefore the 10yr yield jumps to a post-2007 high of 5.11% in its biggest one-day move since April 2025, therefore equities sell off despite the strong data because valuations can't hold at that yield level. Secondary JPM chain: the same PMI/oil/technical-level factors plus a weak 5Y auction (3.20bp tail, disappointing 'end user' demand) drive the day's yield spike (17537); separately (17539, a different desk/date), JPM argues yields are moving toward a 5.5% fair-value anchor and recommends buying this dip because similar overshoots have been buying opportunities, cushioned by valuations and a possible geopolitical off-ramp -- no source ties the auction result to testing that fair-value thesis, and JPM's Sep 21 cautious-equity stance is attributed by JPM itself to energy prices, elevated bond vol, and unclear positioning, not to 'needing more yield pain before its buy level arrives.'
pulse_chain: PMI beat -> yield spike to 5.11%/5.16% -> valuations break -> hike pricing (37bps, 71% October) -> disinflation assumption removed -> Fed can't talk long yields down. Then: JPMorgan reads the selloff as an entry point at a 5.5% fair-value anchor, but 'needs more yield pain before its buy level arrives, which is why its own near-term equity stance is cautious into the Fed meeting'; Wednesday's weak five-year auction is presented as 'the tell' -- had 5.11% been genuinely cheap against 5.5%, real money would have bought the auction, and it didn't, so the invalidation is whether 5.5% gets hit as overshoot-to-buy or repricing-to-respect.
why: The pulse invents a causal link -- that the weak 5Y auction 'tests' and undercuts JPMorgan's own 5.5%-fair-value buy-the-dip thesis, and that this is why JPM's equity stance is cautious -- which appears in neither JPM note; 17537 reports the auction only as one of four generic drivers of the day's yield move, and 17539's fair-value/buy-the-dip case and 17537's own list of reasons for caution (energy prices, bond vol, positioning) never connect to the auction result at all, making the theme's invalidation logic a pulse-authored mechanism dressed as JPMorgan's reasoning.
